# Finite Abelian Subgroups of the Cremona Group: Proofs and Structural Results

This article is devoted to establishing rigorous proofs for a collection of results that were previously announced concerning finite Abelian subgroups of the Cremona group of the plane. In addition to furnishing complete demonstrations of these earlier claims, the work provides detailed descriptions of automorphisms of rational surfaces, thereby situating the algebraic study of the Cremona group within a broader geometric framework.

## A Criterion for Conjugacy to Automorphisms of Minimal Surfaces

A central contribution of the paper is the development of a systematic method for determining whether a given finite Abelian subgroup of the Cremona group is birationally conjugate to a group of automorphisms acting on a minimal surface. This criterion serves as a foundational tool throughout the paper, allowing one to reduce questions about abstract birational transformations to more tractable questions about automorphisms of well-understood geometric objects. The method exploits the classification of minimal rational surfaces and their automorphism groups, providing a bridge between the birational geometry of the plane and the biregular geometry of its minimal models.

## Linearisability of Finite Cyclic Groups

Building on this framework, the article proves a precise characterization of when a finite cyclic group of birational transformations of the plane is linearisable—that is, conjugate to a group of linear automorphisms of the projective plane. The result states that such a group is linearisable if and only if none of its non-trivial elements fixes a curve of positive genus. This theorem gives a clean, checkable geometric criterion for linearisability, translating an algebraic property (conjugacy to a linear action) into a condition on fixed loci that can, in principle, be verified through direct geometric inspection of the transformations involved.

## An Exceptional Case Among Abelian Groups

Despite the elegance of the cyclic case, the paper reveals that the situation is more subtle when one passes to Abelian groups that are not cyclic. Specifically, a striking exception is identified: there exists a finite Abelian group isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}$ all of whose non-trivial elements fail to fix any curve of positive genus, and yet the group itself is *not* conjugate to a group of automorphisms of any minimal rational surface. This example demonstrates that the natural generalization of the cyclic linearisability criterion does not extend to the broader class of Abelian groups, highlighting an unexpected obstruction that arises purely from the group-theoretic structure of the Abelian group in question rather than from the geometric behavior of any single element. This exception underscores the necessity of the more refined conjugacy criterion developed earlier in the paper, since a naive fixed-curve criterion is insufficient once one moves beyond cyclic groups.

## Automorphisms of Del Pezzo Surfaces and Conic Bundles

Finally, the article extends its scope beyond finite subgroups by offering detailed descriptions of automorphisms—not necessarily of finite order—for two important classes of rational surfaces: del Pezzo surfaces and conic bundles. These descriptions complement the finite group results and provide a more complete picture of the automorphism groups that can arise on minimal rational surfaces, situating the study of finite Abelian subgroups within the wider context of the full automorphism groups of these surfaces. This broader perspective is essential for understanding how finite subgroups sit inside, and interact with, the full birational automorphism structure of rational surfaces.

# Finite Abelian Subgroups of the Cremona Group of the Plane

## Introduction and Background

The Cremona group $\mathrm{Cr}_2(\mathbb{C})$, consisting of birational transformations of the projective plane $\mathbb{P}^2$, has long been a central object of study in algebraic geometry, particularly with respect to its finite subgroups. A fundamental question in this area concerns **linearisation**: given a finite subgroup $G \subset \mathrm{Cr}_2(\mathbb{C})$, one asks whether $G$ is conjugate, within the Cremona group, to a subgroup of $\mathrm{PGL}_3(\mathbb{C})$—that is, whether the birational action of $G$ on $\mathbb{P}^2$ can be birationally transformed into a genuinely linear (projective) action.

This article addresses this question systematically for finite **Abelian** subgroups of $\mathrm{Cr}_2(\mathbb{C})$, extending and refining earlier work on cyclic groups and providing a comprehensive framework applicable to more general Abelian group actions. The approach rests on the classical Minimal Model Program perspective: any finite subgroup $G \subset \mathrm{Cr}_2(\mathbb{C})$ can be realized as a group of biregular automorphisms of some smooth projective rational surface $X$, and by running an appropriate $G$-equivariant Minimal Model Program, one arrives at a $G$-minimal model. Such a minimal model is either a **del Pezzo surface** (with $\mathrm{Pic}(X)^G$ of rank one) or admits a **conic bundle structure** $X \to \mathbb{P}^1$ compatible with the $G$-action (with $\mathrm{Pic}(X)^G$ of rank two, and $G$ acting non-trivially on the base).

## Methodology

A key contribution of the article is the development of an effective and conceptually clear **method for determining birational conjugacy** of a finite Abelian subgroup $G \subset \mathrm{Cr}_2(\mathbb{C})$ to a subgroup of automorphisms of a minimal rational surface—namely $\mathbb{P}^2$, a Hirzebruch surface $\mathbb{F}_n$, or a smooth quadric. The strategy proceeds by:

1. **Classifying $G$-minimal surfaces.** For each isomorphism type of finite Abelian group $G$, the possible $G$-minimal rational surfaces (del Pezzo surfaces of various degrees, and conic bundles with varying numbers of singular fibres) on which $G$ can act are enumerated, together with explicit descriptions of the induced action on cohomology and on geometric invariants such as fixed points and fixed curves.

2. **Analyzing fixed loci.** For automorphisms of del Pezzo surfaces and of conic bundles, the article gives detailed descriptions of the fixed-point loci and, crucially, of **curves of fixed points**. Since birational maps between smooth rational surfaces are compositions of blow-ups and blow-downs at points, and blowing up or down a point does not change the birational type of curves fixed pointwise by an automorphism (away from finitely many points), the genus of curves fixed by elements of $G$ is a **birational invariant** of the pair $(X, G)$. This observation is central to the method: if some non-trivial element of $G$ fixes a curve of positive genus on one $G$-minimal model, this remains true for every birational model, obstructing conjugacy to a linear action (since linear actions on $\mathbb{P}^2$ only fix lines and, in special cases, smooth conics—both of genus zero).

3. **Constructing explicit linearisations.** Conversely, when no element of $G$ fixes a curve of positive genus, the article constructs explicit birational maps—often via classical constructions such as blowing down exceptional configurations, or exploiting the geometry of pencils of curves invariant under $G$—that conjugate the action into $\mathrm{PGL}_3(\mathbb{C})$ or into the automorphism group of a Hirzebruch surface.

This two-pronged approach—genus-of-fixed-curve obstruction versus explicit construction—forms the backbone of the classification.

## Main Results

Applying this method to the case of **cyclic groups**, the article establishes the following clean criterion:

> **Theorem.** A finite cyclic subgroup $G = \langle g \rangle \subset \mathrm{Cr}_2(\mathbb{C})$ is linearisable if and only if no non-trivial element of $G$ fixes a curve of positive genus.

This confirms, in a unified and self-contained way, that the fixed-curve genus condition is not merely necessary (as follows from the birational invariance argument above) but also **sufficient** for cyclic groups, resolving the question completely in this case.

However, when the analysis is extended to general finite **Abelian** groups, the situation is more subtle. The article demonstrates that the same fixed-curve criterion, while still necessary for linearisation, is **no longer sufficient** in general. Precisely one exceptional isomorphism type of Abelian group arises:

> **Theorem (Exceptional case).** There exists a finite subgroup $G \subset \mathrm{Cr}_2(\mathbb{C})$, isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}$, such that no non-trivial element of $G$ fixes a curve of positive genus, yet $G$ is **not** conjugate in $\mathrm{Cr}_2(\mathbb{C})$ to a subgroup of automorphisms of $\mathbb{P}^2$, a Hirzebruch surface, or any other minimal rational surface.

This group is realized as a subgroup of automorphisms of a $G$-minimal conic bundle (or del Pezzo surface, depending on the specific model), and the obstruction to its conjugacy to a minimal model action is of a more delicate nature than the genus obstruction: it is detected instead through finer invariants related to the structure of the $G$-equivariant Sarkisov program connecting different $G$-minimal models, and to the impossibility of eliminating certain **Sarkisov links** while preserving the group action.

## Significance

The identification of this single exceptional case is notable precisely because it shows that the elegant genus-of-fixed-curves criterion, which fully characterises linearisability for cyclic groups, breaks down—in as mild a way as possible—once one passes to Abelian groups with more than one generator. The article's careful classification of $G$-minimal del Pezzo surfaces and conic bundles for all finite Abelian groups, together with the explicit identification of this unique obstruction, provides a complete resolution of the linearisation problem for finite Abelian subgroups of $\mathrm{Cr}_2(\mathbb{C})$, and offers a template method applicable more broadly to the study of finite subgroups of the Cremona group of the plane.

# This, Blanc, Finite

There is something quietly profound in the word "this"—a pointer, a gesture toward a fleeting moment, an object, or a feeling that exists here, now, and nowhere else. When we say "this," we anchor ourselves to the present, however briefly, before the moment slips into memory.

Blanc—the French word for white, for blank—carries its own weight of meaning. A blank page holds infinite possibility before the first mark is made. It is the color of snow before footprints, of canvas before paint, of silence before sound. Mont Blanc, the towering peak that borders France and Italy, embodies this whiteness literally: eternal snow crowning a mountain that has watched centuries pass beneath its frozen gaze. Yet even mountains, for all their apparent permanence, are not eternal. They erode, shift, and will one day crumble into dust, reshaped by forces greater than themselves.

This brings us to finite—the boundary that defines all things we know. Our lives are finite. Our resources are finite. Even the universe, vast as it seems, may have its limits, whether in space, time, or possibility. To be finite is to have an edge, a place where something ends and something else begins, or where nothing begins at all.

Perhaps the connection between these three ideas lies in their relationship to time and presence. "This" moment we experience is itself finite—it cannot last, cannot be held indefinitely, no matter how much we wish to freeze it like snow on a mountain peak. The blank page of the future becomes marked with the ink of lived experience, and eventually, that page too reaches its final line.

There is a strange comfort in recognizing the finite nature of things. It gives weight to "this" moment, this blank canvas we are given each day. Because it will end, because it is limited, it matters. The white expanse of unwritten possibility that stretches before us is precious precisely because it is not infinite—we must choose what to write upon it, what mark to leave, before the page runs out.

In embracing the finite, we learn to cherish the immediacy of "this"—this breath, this thought, this fleeting instant of blank potential, waiting to be filled before time closes the book.

# Abstract

We provide complete proofs of results previously announced concerning finite Abelian subgroups of the Cremona group $\mathrm{Cr}_2(\mathbb{C})$ of birational transformations of the projective plane. Our approach relies on the minimal model program for rational $G$-surfaces, which reduces the classification problem to the study of Abelian group actions on del Pezzo surfaces and conic bundles.

We establish a complete linearisability criterion for finite cyclic subgroups of $\mathrm{Cr}_2(\mathbb{C})$: a cyclic subgroup is conjugate to a subgroup of $\mathrm{PGL}_3(\mathbb{C})$ if and only if it satisfies an explicit numerical condition on its fixed points and their local eigenvalues, formulated in terms of the action on the Picard lattice and the associated root system data. This criterion is effective and allows one to decide linearisability directly from the character of the representation on a resolution of the action.

To obtain this classification we give a detailed description of the automorphism groups of del Pezzo surfaces of every degree, determining for each degree the possible finite Abelian subgroups of $\mathrm{Aut}(X)$ together with normal forms for the corresponding surfaces and explicit equations. We similarly describe the finite Abelian subgroups of automorphisms of conic bundles, including the interplay between the action on the base curve and on the fibers, and the associated bi-degree and discriminant data.

Combining these two descriptions with the classification of Sarkisov links between rational $G$-surfaces, we obtain a complete list, up to conjugacy in $\mathrm{Cr}_2(\mathbb{C})$, of finite Abelian subgroups of the plane Cremona group, together with a description of their possible embeddings and the birational superrigidity or non-rigidity of the corresponding models. As an application we recover and refine earlier partial results on conjugacy classes of finite cyclic and Abelian groups of small order, and we clarify several subtle points in the existing literature regarding exceptional cases in low degree.

# Abstract

In a previous Comptes Rendus note, we announced classification results concerning finite abelian subgroups of the Cremona group $\mathrm{Cr}_n(\mathbb{k})$ of birational transformations of $\mathbb{P}^n$ over an algebraically closed field $\mathbb{k}$. The present article provides complete proofs of these results, together with several refinements and additional examples that clarify the geometry underlying the classification.

We focus primarily on the case $n=2$, giving a detailed birational classification of finite abelian subgroups of $\mathrm{Cr}_2(\mathbb{k})$ up to conjugacy. Our approach rests on the Minimal Model Program for surfaces equipped with a group action: given a finite abelian subgroup $G \subset \mathrm{Cr}_2(\mathbb{k})$, we show that a suitable birational model of $\mathbb{P}^2$ on which $G$ acts biregularly can always be reduced, through a sequence of $G$-equivariant contractions, to one of a short list of minimal $G$-surfaces — namely $G$-conic bundles and $G$-del Pezzo surfaces of bounded degree. We then analyze the possible groups $G$ arising in each case, determining the constraints imposed by the geometry of the surface (Picard rank, configuration of exceptional curves, orbits of singular fibers, etc.) and by the requirement that $G$ act by automorphisms.

For the case of cyclic groups, we recover and extend known results, identifying the maximal such groups and the surfaces on which they act minimally. For non-cyclic abelian groups, in particular groups of the form $(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^2$ and their generalizations, we obtain new classification statements, describing precisely which groups embed into $\mathrm{Cr}_2(\mathbb{k})$, the possible actions up to conjugacy, and the associated invariants (such as the surfaces realizing them as automorphism groups and the corresponding fixed-point data). Particular attention is paid to fields of positive characteristic, where additional phenomena — arising from wild ramification and from the modular behavior of certain group schemes — produce subgroups and configurations with no characteristic-zero analogue; we determine exactly when such phenomena occur.

We also discuss the question of realizing abstract abelian groups as subgroups of $\mathrm{Cr}_2(\mathbb{k})$, giving explicit bounds on the rank and exponent of finite abelian subgroups in terms of $\mathbb{k}$, and we describe representative embeddings for each group appearing in our classification. Throughout, we illustrate the classification with explicit examples of $G$-conic bundles and $G$-del Pezzo surfaces, exhibiting equations and explicit generators of $G$ realizing each case in the list.

The results obtained give a complete answer, in the abelian case, to the problem of classifying finite subgroups of the Cremona group of the plane up to conjugation, and provide tools and a template for the study of the non-abelian case, which will be treated in subsequent work.

1. **Linearisability criterion for cyclic groups.** The paper establishes necessary and sufficient conditions under which a finite cyclic subgroup of Bir(P²) is linearisable, i.e., conjugate to a subgroup of PGL(3). The analysis relies on the classification of finite-order birational transformations via their action on minimal rational surfaces (through the minimal model program for pairs), examining the possible fixed loci, invariant curves, and the structure of the quotient.

# On the Conjugacy of Finite Abelian Subgroups of the Cremona Group to Automorphisms of Minimal Rational Surfaces

## Abstract

Let $G$ be a finite abelian subgroup of the Cremona group $\mathrm{Cr}_2(\mathbb{C})$ of birational transformations of $\mathbb{P}^2_{\mathbb{C}}$. We investigate the conditions under which $G$ is conjugate, within $\mathrm{Cr}_2(\mathbb{C})$, to a subgroup of automorphisms of a minimal rational surface $X$, that is, a surface equipped with a $G$-Mori fiber space structure: either a del Pezzo surface with $\mathrm{Pic}(X)^G \cong \mathbb{Z}$, or a conic bundle with $\mathrm{Pic}(X)^G \cong \mathbb{Z}^2$.

We establish that the birational classification of such $G$-actions is governed by an invariant curve criterion: the existence of a $G$-invariant curve $C \subset \mathbb{P}^2$ (or its transform on a blow-up) whose geometric genus and the induced action of $G$ on $C$ remain invariant under $G$-equivariant birational transformations. Specifically, we show that a finite abelian subgroup $G \subset \mathrm{Cr}_2(\mathbb{C})$ is uniquely determined up to conjugacy by the following birational invariants:

1. the isomorphism type of the abstract group $G$,
2. the genus $g$ of a minimal $G$-invariant curve of maximal genus fixed pointwise or preserved setwise by the induced $G$-action, together with the character by which $G$ acts on $H^0(C, \omega_C)$ when $g \geq 1$,
3. the topological type of the fixed locus $X^G$ on the associated minimal model $X$.

The main theorem asserts that if $G$ fixes a curve of genus $g \geq 1$, this genus, together with the linearization data of the $G$-action on the curve, determines the conjugacy class of $G$ in $\mathrm{Cr}_2(\mathbb{C})$ up to a finite and explicitly bounded ambiguity arising from the choice of minimal model. We further show that two such subgroups $G_1, G_2$ realizing isomorphic actions on curves of the same genus $g \geq 2$ are conjugate in $\mathrm{Cr}_2(\mathbb{C})$ if and only if the corresponding minimal del Pezzo or conic bundle models are $G$-equivariantly birational, a condition verified explicitly via the Sarkisov program for surfaces with $G$-action.

A notable **exceptional case** arises for $G \cong (\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^2$ or $G \cong \mathbb{Z}/6\mathbb{Z}$ acting with a fixed curve of genus $1$: here the naive genus-and-character invariant fails to distinguish conjugacy classes, and an additional discrete invariant — related to the number and configuration of base points of the associated linear system, or equivalently to the class of the extension in $H^1(G, \mathrm{Jac}(C))$ — must be introduced. In this exceptional situation, we exhibit two non-conjugate embeddings of $G$ into $\mathrm{Cr}_2(\mathbb{C})$ that induce isomorphic actions on invariant genus-one curves but are not conjugate to automorphisms of the same minimal del Pezzo surface, thereby demonstrating that the genus criterion, while necessary, is not in general sufficient without this supplementary arithmetic datum.

# Abstract

This paper provides complete proofs of the results announced in our earlier Comptes Rendus note, concerning the linearisability of finite abelian group actions on rational surfaces. We investigate when a birational action of a cyclic or abelian group on a rational surface is conjugate, in the Cremona group, to a linear action on the projective plane.

Our approach proceeds through the equivariant Minimal Model Program, reducing the study to actions on relatively minimal models—del Pezzo surfaces and conic bundles—invariant under the group action. For each family of minimal models, we analyse the possible group actions arising from their automorphism groups and determine precise numerical and geometric criteria, expressed in terms of fixed points, invariant curves, and the structure of the Picard lattice, under which the action is linearisable.

For cyclic groups, we give a complete classification of linearisable actions on rational surfaces, identifying obstructions arising from non-linearisable actions on del Pezzo surfaces of small degree and on conic bundles with prescribed singular fibre configurations. We extend these criteria to abelian groups of higher rank, addressing new phenomena arising from the interplay between multiple independent generators, including obstructions that are not detected by cyclic subgroups alone.

The results yield explicit examples distinguishing linearisable and non-linearisable actions, clarify the boundary cases left open in the announcement, and establish a coherent classification framework for finite abelian subgroups of the Cremona group of rank two up to conjugacy.
